clue.text: Thank God it's this helpful man!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the day celebrated in the office saying TGIF, the end of the working week
second meaning: Man ..., Crusoe's loyal servant, so a faithful assistant

explanation.surface: Someone gives heartfelt thanks to the heavens for a helpful fellow who turned up.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'Thank God it's Friday' supplies the first meaning; Robinson Crusoe's servant Man Friday gives the second, which is why a general helper is called a man Friday.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses rest on one weekday name: the cheering end of the working week and the loyal servant in Defoe's novel.

clue.text: Blue-black crow loses tail in storm

indicators.note: losing its tail means the bird's name gives up its final letter

parts.note: a raven is a large glossy blue-black member of the crow family

explanation.surface: A bird caught in bad weather has its tail feathers ripped away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Storm' looks like the weather the crow is caught in, but it is the verb meaning to rant furiously.
explanation.definitionFit: To rave is to shout wildly and angrily, which is what someone does when they storm at others.

clue.text: Here's the target: tuck, meals

parts.note: in dressmaking a dart is a stitched tuck that shapes a garment
board means meals provided, as in board and lodging

explanation.surface: A greedy diner announces that food and goodies are what they are aiming for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tuck' is British schoolboy slang for snacks and sweets, which pairs naturally with 'meals'; here it is the sewing term instead.
explanation.definitionFit: The round board players throw darts at is literally the thing aimed at in a pub game.

clue.text: Try tea brewed like this to make you babble

indicators.note: brewing mixes ingredients together, so the letters of the two words are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An invitation to sample a cup of tea made a certain way, promising it will set you chattering.
explanation.walkthrough: Yatter is informal, chiefly Scottish and northern British, for idle chatter.
explanation.definitionFit: To yatter is to talk incessantly about trivial things, the same as babbling on.

clue.text: Girl anyway seen in church after ten for afternoon diversion

indicators.note: following on means the girl's name is written second, behind the number
arranged any way you like, so the letters may be set down in a different order

parts.note: the number written as a word
a common crossword girl's name
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A girl turns up at church after ten o'clock, looking for some way to pass the afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anyway' reads as a casual filler word but tells you to rearrange the girl and the number; the church abbreviation then follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea dance is an afternoon social with dancing and refreshments, a genteel diversion between lunch and dinner.

clue.text: To say something indiscreet is to perform an awkward manoeuvre

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the idiom for making a tactless blunder in speech
second meaning: taken literally, a feat needing great physical contortion

annotation.spelling: TO PUT ONE'S FOOT IN ONE'S MOUTH

explanation.surface: A definition-style statement equating a social gaffe with a physical contortion.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom is read once as a figure of speech and once literally, as a gymnastic feat.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes blurting out a tactless remark, and read literally it is a difficult bodily contortion.

clue.text: Heês changed his views in a Post Office report

parts.note: taken as written
PO is the standard abbreviation for Post Office
to state is to report or declare

explanation.surface: Someone announces a change of heart in an official post office report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' looks like a noun naming a document, but it is the verb meaning declare.
explanation.definitionFit: An apostate is a person who renounces a former religious or political belief, someone whose views have shifted.

clue.text: I'm unhappy! I have a deficiency

parts.note: taken as written
a lack is a deficiency or shortage

explanation.surface: Someone complains of being miserable because something is missing from their life.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface links the two halves as cause and effect; really one half is an old cry of sorrow and the other spells it out.
explanation.definitionFit: Alack is an archaic exclamation of regret or sorrow, a cry expressing that the speaker is miserable.

clue.text: Innocence shown by well-scrubbed crew

parts.note: something well scrubbed is clean
a ship's crew are its hands

explanation.surface: A spotless ship's crew are taken as evidence that nobody aboard did wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: Having clean hands is the idiom for being free of guilt.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes freedom from guilt or wrongdoing, so the phrase stands for blamelessness.

clue.text: Repairing vest with rope is to transgress

indicators.note: repairing means remaking something, so the letters are put back together in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Mending an undershirt with a length of cord is apparently against the rules.
explanation.definitionFit: To overstep is to go beyond an allowed limit, which is the literal sense of transgressing a boundary.

clue.text: "Yes, a company needs to be turned round", says Irish dramatist

indicators.note: turning something round faces it the other way, so the letters are read from the end

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
CO is the abbreviation for company; that its letters also begin the word is a coincidence, not a hidden word

explanation.surface: An Irish playwright agrees that a failing firm must be rescued and turned around.
explanation.walkthrough: Sean O'Casey wrote Juno and the Paycock and The Plough and the Stars.
explanation.definitionFit: Sean O'Casey was a twentieth-century playwright from Dublin, famous for his Abbey Theatre plays.

clue.text: Bather in distress, suffering. How exciting!

definitions.note: an exclamation describing the answer's quality rather than an adjective

indicators.note: something in distress is disordered and agitated, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
'in a taking' is an old phrase for being agitated or distressed

explanation.surface: A swimmer in difficulties is struggling, and a spectator finds the drama thrilling.
explanation.walkthrough: A taking is an old word for a state of agitation or suffering.
explanation.definitionFit: Something breathtaking is so thrilling or astonishing it stops your breath, the reaction voiced by that exclamation.

clue.text: Chance for tennis player to change pink boater

indicators.note: changing the words means rearranging their letters into something new

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tennis player gets the opportunity to swap a pink straw hat for something else.
explanation.walkthrough: A boater is a flat-topped straw hat, often worn at summer events.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis, a break point is the receiving player's opportunity to win a game on the opponent's serve.

clue.text: Callas losing head in "Your tiny hand is frozen"?

indicators.note: losing its head means the singer's first name drops its first letter

parts.note: Maria Callas was the celebrated twentieth-century operatic soprano

explanation.surface: A famous soprano is overcome while singing a well-known Puccini number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Your tiny hand is frozen' (Che gelida manina) is Rodolfo's tenor solo from Puccini's La Bohème; the question mark marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Puccini piece is a celebrated solo song from an opera, an instance of the operatic form.

clue.text: Antlion with a fickle public

indicators.note: fickle means changeable, so the letters do not stay in their given order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An insect is said to be in league with a public that keeps changing its mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Public' looks like the noun after 'fickle', but it is the adjective being defined.
explanation.definitionFit: Something national belongs to the whole country rather than a private party, which is one sense of public, as in public ownership.

clue.text: See 5
Member all but hiding published sheet

indicators.note: hiding something means wrapping it out of sight, so one word sits inside the other
all but means everything except the last bit, so the final letter goes

parts.note: taken as written
a newspaper that ran a story published it

explanation.surface: A club member conceals almost everything about a paper they have printed.
explanation.walkthrough: The shortened member is split around the publishing word.
explanation.definitionFit: A membrane is a thin pliable layer of tissue or material, a sheet in the sense of a thin covering.

clue.text: Jailer in battle costume

parts.note: war is armed fighting, a battle
dress is clothing or costume

explanation.surface: A prison guard is pictured dressed up in combat gear.
explanation.definitionFit: A wardress is a female prison officer, an old British term for a woman who guards inmates.

clue.text: Suspends only half of one's objectives

indicators.note: only half of the word is used, so the answer sits inside it as its second half

parts.note: the back four of its eight letters

explanation.surface: Someone halts only some of their aims, putting half of them on hold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspends' looks like the verb of the sentence, but it is the word to be halved.
explanation.definitionFit: Ends in the sense of aims or goals, as in 'the ends justify the means', are things you strive for.

clue.text: Long snake put down with anger

parts.note: an asp is a small venomous snake
ire is a literary word for anger

explanation.surface: A long snake is killed in a fit of rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' looks like an adjective for the snake, but it is the verb meaning yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: To aspire is to yearn or have ambitions for something, which matches the verb sense of longing.

clue.text: Musical time for togetherness converted Pope and Lamb about bereavement

definitions.note: the answer is the noun phrase that precedes 'time' in the song title

indicators.note: about means around, so the rearranged names surround the grief word
converted means turned into something else, so the two names are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
a bereavement is the loss of a loved one

explanation.surface: Two literary figures, the poet Alexander Pope and Charles Lamb, are transformed while surrounding a death.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points to the song 'I'll Be With You in Apple Blossom Time', whose title promises a reunion.
explanation.definitionFit: The popular song pledges that the lovers will be together when the orchard trees flower in spring.

clue.text: One carried by old railway and Titanic?

indicators.note: carried by means held within, so the railway's letters enclose the numeral

parts.note: the London and North Eastern Railway, a British company merged into British Railways in 1948
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A traveller's journey on a historic train and then on the doomed ship.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark shows the definition is an example: the Titanic was a famous ocean liner.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titanic was a large passenger ship on a regular transatlantic route, the classic example of an ocean liner.

clue.text: Vehicle: one attracting a levy

indicators.note: attracting means drawing something in towards itself, so the numeral sits beside the duty word

parts.note: a tax is a levy
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A vehicle is described as the sort that gets hit with a duty.
explanation.definitionFit: A taxi is a car hired with a driver for single journeys, a kind of road vehicle.

clue.text: City of music where the Queen returns after six

indicators.note: after means placed behind, so the queen comes second, behind the number

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the queen's name is read from the end

parts.note: Queen Anne reigned from 1702 to 1714

explanation.surface: A queen comes back to a musical city after six o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Queen' here is not ER but the earlier monarch Anne, read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Vienna was home to Mozart, Haydn, Beethoven, Schubert and the Strauss family, a capital famous for classical music.

clue.text: Pain in the neck conceals hairstyle, so Iêm hearing

indicators.note: concealing something means holding it out of sight, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: an annoying person or thing is a trial
a bun is hair coiled into a knot at the back of the head

explanation.surface: Someone with a sore neck hides it under their hairdo and notices only what they hear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearing' seems to be what the speaker is doing, but it is the noun for a formal inquiry.
explanation.definitionFit: A tribunal is a body set up to judge disputes, and a hearing is the formal session in which it does so.

clue.text: Large fish when turning round shows no e.g. tracks

indicators.note: turning round means facing back, so the words are read from right to left

parts.note: taken as written
the abbreviation for 'for example', taken without its dots
ruts are tracks worn into the ground by wheels

explanation.surface: A big fish swims round in circles and leaves no trail behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Every letter of the last three words is used, written backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The sturgeon is a very large river and sea fish, the source of caviar.

clue.text: Repetitive selection if only the first were last

indicators.text: if only the first were last
indicators.note: swapping which end comes first means one letter jumps from the end of the word to its front

parts.note: a choice is a selection

explanation.surface: Someone wistfully wishes a repetitive list had a different order.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads oddly: the last letter of the word becomes its first, so what was last is now first.
explanation.definitionFit: Echoic describes something that imitates or repeats a sound, like an echo, hence repeating or imitative.
